question_text: When building a decoupling network, why do we use capacitors spaced a "decade" apart in value and physical package size (e.g., 1µF in 0402 alongside 0.1µF in 0201)?
answer_text: Spacing them by a decade in value and shrinking the physical size for the smaller capacitors creates overlapping SRF curves, pushing high-frequency noise filtering much further out.
explanation_text: The physical footprint of a capacitor dominates its parasitic Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL). A tiny 0201 package has drastically lower ESL than a larger 0402 package. Because SRF is the point where capacitance and ESL cancel out, lowering the ESL pushes the SRF to much higher frequencies. A 1µF 0402 provides good mid-frequency bulk decoupling, but its larger ESL makes it fail (turn inductive) at high frequencies. Placing an ultra-low ESL 0.1µF 0201 in parallel covers those higher frequencies perfectly.
bonus_question_text: On an Impedance vs. Frequency plot, what does the combined impedance of these parallel capacitors look like?
bonus_answer_text: Because they are in parallel, the total impedance follows the path of least resistance. The individual V-shaped SRF curves intersect, and the overall impedance "rides" the bottom outline of those intersecting curves, forming a broad low-impedance trough.
